title: Fake Egypt Tour Companies: 9 Red Flags to Spot
excerpt: Nine red flags of fake Egypt tour companies, from cloned sites and WhatsApp-only sellers to transfer-only payment, plus chargeback steps if you have already paid.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

Quick answer

The nine warning signs: cloned websites on lookalike domains, WhatsApp-only sellers, bank-transfer-only payment, missing licence numbers, too-perfect reviews, too-good-to-be-true prices, pressure tactics, no company footprint, and bookings that never name the operating company. Your two defences are simple: pay by card, and book only operators that publish their licence and their name. Here is each flag, and what to do if you have already paid.

The Egyptian Travel Agents Association provides an independent place to check agency membership.

Key facts

Fact Detail
What legitimate shows A named operating company, a Ministry of Tourism licence and ETAA registration, card payments accepted, published booking terms, a verifiable review history
What fraud shows Cloned or weeks-old domains, chat-only contact, bank-transfer-only payment, no licence number, clusters of five-star reviews
Chargeback window Card disputes are commonly allowed for about 120 days from the transaction, sometimes longer for services not yet delivered. Start immediately and ask your card issuer
Where to report Your bank or card issuer, the tourist police on 126 if you are in Egypt, your embassy, and your home country's fraud service
Check a company on Sawa Every departure names its operating agency, one of the licensed Egyptian agencies with travellers on the date, before your deposit is due. How agencies are checked is on the verify page

The nine red flags

Egypt's licensed tour industry is real, regulated and very good at what it does. Around its edges operates a scam layer that preys on exactly the travellers this blog is written for: first-timers booking from abroad, paying deposits to people they have never met. The gap between the two is not luck. It is a set of visible signals, nine of which appear again and again. This guide lists them, shows how to verify a company in ten minutes, and gives the recovery steps if money has already moved. We are the people behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure platform, and we have worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

  1. Cloned websites. A copy of a real agency's site, hosted on a domain one letter off: an extra hyphen, .net instead of .com. The design looks familiar; the booking form sends your money somewhere new. Check the exact domain spelling, and look up when the domain was registered. A domain lookup (WHOIS) usually shows the registration date, and a big agency on a domain registered weeks ago is a warning in itself.
  2. WhatsApp-only sellers. The entire business lives in one chat thread: no website, no office, no phone number that resolves to a company. Legitimate operators can be contacted at least two ways and in writing. A seller who exists only in your chat list exists nowhere.
  3. Bank-transfer-only payment. "Pay by transfer to this personal account" removes your single strongest protection, the card chargeback, and a personal account is not a company. Legitimate platforms publish their payment terms and never insist on transfer alone.
  4. Missing licence number. Egyptian tour operators are licensed by the Ministry of Tourism and registered with the Egyptian Travel Agents Association (ETAA). A company that shows neither, and cannot name the operating company that would actually run your tour, is not a company you can hold accountable later.
  5. Fake reviews. Five-star clusters dated within days of each other, generic wording that could describe any country, reviewers with no other history. Read the negatives and the dates, not the score.
  6. Too-good-to-be-true prices. The same Nile cruise or pyramid day at half the going rate is not a deal; it is the hook. Real operators' prices sit within a band, and a quote far below it is one of the clearest scam signals of all.
  7. Pressure tactics. "Today only", "last seat", "the price rises tonight": urgency exists to stop you from running the checks in the next section. A real operator's offer survives until tomorrow.
  8. No company footprint. No street address, no company registration, a generic email address on a weeks-old domain. Real businesses leave trails; check the address exists and the company is registered.
  9. No named operating company on the booking. You pay, and you still don't know who actually runs the tour. A legitimate booking names the operating company on the departure page, in the terms and on the confirmation.

How to verify an Egypt tour company in ten minutes

Run the positive checks against any operator before money moves:

  • Ask for the Ministry of Tourism licence number and the ETAA registration, and check they match what the company shows on its own website and terms. You can also ask ETAA about a member.
  • Confirm the company registration and the street address exist.
  • Look up the domain's registration date.
  • Read the review history rather than the review score.
  • Test that card payment is genuinely offered.
  • Call the listed number.

Ten minutes of checking filters out nearly everything on the list above. The fuller method is in our guide to checking an Egypt tour company's licence.

Already paid? Chargeback steps and reporting routes

If the signals clicked into place only after you paid, act immediately. Recovery is time-sensitive, and the steps below work best in the first days.

  1. Dispute the charge with your bank or card issuer now. Say "fraudulent transaction" and "I want to dispute this charge".
  2. Know the window. Card disputes are commonly allowed for about 120 days from the transaction, and sometimes longer where the service has not yet been delivered. Your own issuer's rules decide, so ask, and do not wait.
  3. Assemble the evidence. Screenshots of the website and chat, the exact URL, transfer receipts, booking confirmations, the seller's phone number and name.
  4. Report the seller to the platform or marketplace you booked through, so the listing dies before the next traveller finds it.
  5. Report to the authorities. The tourist police on 126 if you are already in Egypt (the general police number is 122), your embassy, and your home country's fraud service: Report Fraud in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (the service that replaced Action Fraud), Police Scotland in Scotland, and the Federal Trade Commission in the US.
  6. Leave the review that warns the next traveller. Detail beats anger: what was promised, what you paid, how it was paid.

One line belongs in bold, because it decides most outcomes: a bank transfer to a personal account is the step that removes nearly all of your protection. That is why transfer-only is red flag 3 and not a footnote.

What legitimate looks like: Sawa's answer

The reason we can write this checklist is that we run our own side of it in public. Sawa Tours is operated by Online Era, registration 148500. Every tour is run by a licensed Egyptian operating agency: before an agency can list, we check the documents and confirm the licence with the Ministry, as the verify page sets out. Sawa has a founding operating partner, Capital Travel Service (licence 2179).

On the booking side, each departure is run by one of the licensed Egyptian agencies with travellers on the date, named before your deposit is due. Reserving a seat is free, needs no card, and nothing is charged before four travellers have reserved the date (the GoAhead). Then you pay a deposit (10% on a day tour, 25% on a package) by a secure payment link from Online Era (General Sales Agent licence 32241); charges are in euros. Sawa never asks you to transfer money to a personal account. The cancellation rules are written down in the terms: on a day tour, more than 48 hours before departure is a full refund, deposit included. The mechanics are in how shared departures work, the GoAhead promise and how the GoAhead works, and the wider question is answered in is Sawa Tours legit?. Run the nine flags on us.

The short version

Nine flags, two defences: cloned sites, WhatsApp-only sellers, transfer-only payments, missing licences, fake reviews, too-cheap quotes, pressure tactics, no footprint, no named operator, against a card in your hand and a licence you can look up. Before you book anyone, including us, run the checks. A real company survives being googled. See how Sawa checks its agencies on the verify page, read the FAQ, or read how shared departures work before you pay anyone anything.

tldr: The nine warning signs: cloned websites on lookalike domains, WhatsApp-only sellers, bank-transfer-only payment, missing licence numbers, too-perfect reviews, too-good-to-be-true prices, pressure tactics, no company footprint, and bookings that never name the operating company. Your two defences are simple: pay by card, and book only operators that publish their licence and their name. Here is each flag, and what to do if you have already paid.

faq.q: What are the most common Egypt tour booking scams?
faq.a: Four appear constantly: cloned websites that imitate a real agency on a lookalike domain; WhatsApp-only sellers who exist only in chat; transfer-only bookings to personal accounts, which remove your chargeback protection; and too-cheap itineraries that vanish after the deposit. All four are visible before payment if you run the nine checks above.

faq.q: Is it safe to pay an Egypt tour company by bank transfer?
faq.a: To a company account, with an invoice, it can be. But a transfer to a personal account, with no card option, is the single biggest red flag. Card payments carry the chargeback fallback; transfers carry almost nothing. If an operator refuses card payment entirely, book with one who doesn't.

faq.q: How do I check if an Egypt tour company is licensed?
faq.a: Ask for the Ministry of Tourism licence details and the ETAA registration, and check they are shown on the company's own site and terms. Licensed operators name the operating company that will run your tour. On Sawa, each departure names its operating agency before your deposit is due, and Sawa confirms each agency's licence with the Ministry before it can list.

faq.q: I paid a fake Egypt tour company. Can I get my money back?
faq.a: Sometimes, if you move fast. Dispute the charge with your bank immediately (card disputes are commonly allowed for about 120 days), assemble your evidence, and report to the platform, the tourist police on 126 if you are in Egypt, and your home country's fraud service. Transfers to personal accounts recover far less often, which is why the payment method is red flag 3.
